clauses.reason: Terminated on 1935-06-14 by statute. S.J. Res. 113 (49 Stat. 375, ch. 246), approved June 14, 1935, provides in section 2: 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed.' It states no effective date other than its approval. Under section 3 of the Act an approved code had legal effect only through 3(b) (its provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, and a violation in or affecting interstate commerce was an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act), 3(c) (the district courts could restrain violations and district attorneys were directed to sue) and 3(f) (each violation was a misdemeanor) (SUPPLEMENT:NIRA3). Section 2 of the resolution repealed that enforcement by description, so from June 14, 1935 the approval had no prospective operative effect. A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935, held 'the code-making authority thus conferred is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power' (SUPPLEMENT:SCHECHTERSYL, SUPPLEMENT:SCHECHTERDEL, SUPPLEMENT:SCHECHTERJDG). That is recorded as a validity characterization (under the doctrine prevailing in 1935 an approval made under an unconstitutional delegation was void from issuance), not as an end date: the judgment did not cancel or withdraw this approval, and the recorded end of its operative effect remains June 14, 1935. The clause is dependent on the code: it has no operative effect apart from the approved code's section 3 effects, so no independent command survives.

The text is complete (operative paragraph, signature, recommendation line and date). Identity: the census register (jobs/domesday-register/output/REGISTER.csv) title 'Executive Order 6346—In the Matter of the Application of the Greensboro Lumber Company and H. A. Taylor, for Certain Exemptions from the Code of Fair Competition for the Lumber and Timber Products Ind' dated 1933-10-20 and the WPA 1944 numbered-list summary 'Application of Greensboro Lumber Co. and H. A. Taylor for certainexemptions from the Code of Fair Competition for the Lumber and Timber Products Industriesdenied. II NRA Codes 696.' agree with the text. original not yet held; replace and re-check quotes when an official copy is retrieved. Operative command: the order denies the application of the Greensboro Lumber Company and H. A. Taylor for an exemption from the minimum wage provided in the Lumber and Timber Products Industries code: 'do order that the application for exemption by the above-named applicants be, and it is hereby, denied.' Clause inventory: the machine inventory is accepted as complete (one clause, the operative paragraph with its signature and recommendation lines). The order is a determination under section 3 of the Act and the July 15, 1933 hearing procedure. It commands no person to act; its only legal consequence is that the applicants stay bound by the code's minimum-wage provision, a consequence that exists only while the code is enforceable. The alternative reading, that a denial is exhausted on signing, is not adopted because the denial's operative content (refusing an exemption from a code that continued to bind) lasted as long as the code's enforceability did. First end: 1935-06-14, by S.J. Res. 113 section 2 (SUPPLEMENT:SJRES113), the first end of a code-dependent clause with no earlier own-terms end and no earlier cancellation, supersession or suspension held. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization and not as the end date.

savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the code before June 14, 1935 (violations, injunctions, convictions, compliance) are completed or accrued effects and are not continued operation of the approval. The section 5 antitrust exemption for a code approved and in effect and for action complying with it during the period (SUPPLEMENT:NIRA5) is accrued to the extent it covers action already taken; the resolution's proviso says the exemption 'shall extend only to agreements and action thereunder' putting section 7(a) requirements into effect or prohibiting practices already unlawful, names agreements rather than codes and states no time limit, and the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the exemption for action taken under codes before June 14, 1935. No held source continues this approval after June 14, 1935, and later statutes that regulated an industry are independent laws.
